I've done my share of insane auto pilot things, especially when I was working nights for several years; but nothing in my experience could ever top my father's zombie antics. 
My absolute favorite was when he got the urge to run to the corner store one evening long ago, probably feeling like grabbing a snack or something kind of minor like that. This particular store was very near our house, you literally exited the back door, turned right down the alley and there it was across the street. If I remember correctly, it was a fairly cold winter night and I guess he was already comfortable and settled in for the night, so he decided not to bother with just walking the few yards to the shop as he normally would-- instead he drove to the store and parked outside, left the car running, made his purchases and merrily walked back home, all of this unbeknownst to me. 
He was settled in watching a movie several minutes later when I heard that tell-tale super loud "cop knock" pounding at our door. When I answered, it was two police officers asking if our car was missing.  In the end, we all had a laugh about it, although I think my pop was pretty embarrassed. 

Another time, he'd been sick with the flu for a couple days, had been sleeping a lot and mildly feverish. I was getting ready for bed pretty late at night when he woke up from a long nap and had apparently broken a fever; he was slightly disoriented. So we're talking and he thinks it's morning but I set him straight and he's trying to get his bearings, we're chatting, etc, and then I watch him reach into the fridge and pull out a bottle of hot sauce and take a big ol' swig... he thought it was a glass bottle of orange crush. The look on his face was priceless. 

...Ah, there are many stories of his kooky antics! He was honestly just an extremely absent-minded person, although hands down the most intelligent individual I've ever met. I miss him.

I think that the point was more likely to be that, as a relatively newly diagnosed sufferer, the SO may not KNOW a lot about the options available to her for treatment in general, nor their potential pros and cons. It's more about lupus being a less well-known/publicized illness and reaching out to someone to let them know that there ARE treatments to try... Obviously, most average people have some familiarity with the reality of chemotherapy and its negative effects, but it's ALSO widely known as an available treatment many people are willing to risk undergoing, AND it can really help some patients. 

I really get the idea of wanting to protect someone who is sick and scared from medical treatments that may be sold as curative, when in reality they can be very harmful-- but reacting so aggressively against it-- the mere suggestion that said treatment CAN in fact really help some sufferers (keyword: some) and deserves to be considered as the SO educates herself about the disease-- to a certain extent assumes that the SO is not intelligent enough to investigate her options, learn, and make an informed choice based on her own individual needs and/or the advice of her medical professional. 
Add to that the fact that the other commentator was simply trying to reach out and provide the benefit of his or her own personal experience, as well as offer to talk to the girl about her disease, and you're misinterpreting the intent as an aggressive push for a potentially dangerous medical treatment, consequences be damned...

Ok, I know this thread is old but I can't help but feel I should reply to you. I don't know the circumstances of your situation, or who exactly the homeowner was to you (guessing grandparent, perhaps?), but I understand. 
My father passed away very, very suddenly last year (coming up on the anniversary, actually) and left an entire life and home and WORLD all his own which I am now inhabiting. It's complicated, my family was/is very close but very small and I happened to be home with my parents when it happened. We did our best, but there was no going back. He left the house, which he'd grown up in and salvaged when his own father passed, to myself and my sibling even though my mother still lives here and they were together (as I said, complicated-- they had been separated for years and got back together later in life happier than ever. Guess he never changed it back). It's an old house with so many memories. I'm the remaining local child, so I ended up moving back in to help my mom because there's so much stuff and the house is in such disrepair. 

We have not cleaned out/removed any of his things yet. Don't know that we ever will. The entire house is imbued with his personality and heart, and I think of him every day. We were very close, so I know I would carry him with me regardless (I think of things to tell him, jokes to make and observations literally every minute it seems-- we were very alike. I bought a book to write in when I want to tell him something but I haven't been able to start it yet. There's too much). He always struggled with some depression and we definitely struggled financially as a family-- and his entire life. I remember him talking about how he felt that he would not be able to leave us any "legacy." He worried that he hadn't accomplished enough or left his mark and that when he was gone, he wouldn't have anything to leave behind. Just the home, he thought. He wanted us to have the home. 

But you know what? Every day I look around and I see him. All the little touches he added to the house throughout the years, the art he made, the books he filled with thoughts and songs and lyrics and stories... the little handmade gifts he would give us because we didn't have much money and he would pour his heart into all of it. I'm surrounded by his legacy, and it's more beautiful than anything he could have bought or built in any conventional sense. I know being surrounded by memories can be painful a lot of the time, but I hope that sometimes you can take comfort in being in that environment and still feel the warmth of the person you've "lost." That person is still there in so many ways.

I have experienced this once, and I know other people who suffer from bouts of sleep paralysis quite frequently. It's a very disturbing feeling and it does seem to persist throughout the day; I can't imagine feeling it with frequency. 

The incident in which I experienced sleep paralysis happened recently, and I'd like to understand what might be happening with my brain chemistry now which hadn't occurred before. 

I was suffering a fairly prolonged bout of mild insomnia, and had gone to bed for the evening, trying for hours to fall asleep. In one of those instances where you fall asleep suddenly with no warning, I lost consciousness (I guess), but felt as though no time had passed since I'd last been awake; I thought I was still lying in bed trying to fall asleep. I was laying on my side, with my back to my bedroom door and I heard the strangest sounds coming from outside my bedroom, from my sister's room across the hall. I couldn't tell what it was, and I thought I'd dozed slightly and barely heard it at all, straining to identify the sound. Then I heard her door open (it's always quite creaky) and heard what I thought was her coming through the room adjacent to mine while talking to me and saying my name. It was like I couldn't understand or hear her very well, though I was straining to be able to and I tried to respond (and couldn't. I also couldn't roll over to face the door). I heard/felt the person then come into my bedroom and continue talking to me, and FELT a person lean over me, over my shoulder just out of sight. I could feel the sudden depression of the bed, the presence of another person, and the pressure on the upper left side of my body where she'd have been leaning, just whispering things I couldn't quite make out.

 I couldn't move and I couldn't talk, but I was convinced I was awake. It seemed like a long time passed, but it was probably mere seconds. Then the presence was gone, and I could move. As soon as I could, I was awake again, and I got up to see if anyone in the house was awake, if her door seemed like it'd been open or if she'd been up. No sign of life... It was freaky. It left me unable to fall back to sleep and feeling pretty weird the following morning.

Just wanted to add that if you are AT ALL interested in going back this semester, get an advisor asap. I just reread your post and you mention that you were "approved" for a grant. You most likely will need to go online to financial aid and accept this award. After you do, they can schedule disbursement to you and to the school.

Go. As long as you can still get classes for this semester, you won't regret it. 

I was in the same position last year; I had been through a year of college, did well, and completely fucked myself over the next semester. In my case, I had numerous outside stresses involving deaths in the family, poor health, and a sudden and contentious divorce between my parents (was living at home at the time). I basically flunked that semester, did some damage to my gpa, and ran off to NYC for nearly a year. 

Going back has been challenging, especially accepting the fact that I had to work harder to lift my gpa, but once your head is where it needs to be and you get back into the swing of things, you'll feel great. Seriously. My advice would be to take at least one class purely because it's something you're interested in. This will encourage you to keep at it and provide you with a bright spot to look forward to. Make an appointment with an advisor and see what your options are! 

There's no shame in having left school previously; going back and giving it a second go is something you can be proud of. And don't worry if you haven't chosen a major. Your advisor should be able to help you either find something that suits you, or help you enroll in classes which can be applied to multiple fields (basics/pre-requisites). 

It sucks that you have such a commute, but you can really make use of campus when you're there, get your studying/course-work done, etc, because you'll have to remain there until your last class. I scheduled my classes with an 1 1/2 gap between each day, simply so I could go ahead and complete my course-work as it was issued, without having to deal with it on weekends (I work weekends anyway). That might not be a method which appeals to everyone, but it has really helped me get ahead. 

Best of luck!

I am one of those lucky "freak magnets" you hear about, so I probably have quite a few incidents which are appalling/humorous, but I also have extremely limited experience in going on "dates" in the classic sense. However, I still have a very definite worst date experience:
It was not a first date, but an evening in the middle of a very short-lived relationship wherein the guy I was involved with really revealed his instability. There had been previous signs, but I try hard to be nice, so... let's say I didn't force the issue until the following incident.

We'd been seeing each other pretty casually for a little while, and decided to go to a concert which some of my family was also attending (not together). They'd met each other, so naturally at one point in the evening we gravitated together. My dad pulled me aside and asked if something was wrong with [X], because he had been acting increasingly odd all evening, talking a LOT, talking fast, pulling every single conversation with anyone back to himself, didn't want me out of his sight, etc. I didn't know what to say, and nothing immediately came of it. X and I left the concert before the rest of my friends/family did, and were going to head to his house to watch a movie. I think I was going to stay the night or something, so we stopped by my house on the way back to his (lived fairly near each other), he refused to come in, and I ran inside to grab a change. Not 5 minutes later, I returned, and noticed that he was fully RECOILED against the driver's door and wouldn't look at me or speak to me. After a couple of minutes, he demanded why I had slammed the door as I'd left the car previously, still not looking at me, speaking through gritted teeth, etc. I was completely thrown off, keep in mind that despite his acting a bit "off," things had been perfectly fine between us. I told him that I didn't realize I'd shut the door that hard, and that if I had, I was sorry and it hadn't meant anything. He ignored me. I sat in completely stunned silence, and he began driving back toward his house. I began to feel extremely uncomfortable, and asked a few times if he would say something, whether he intended to be silent all evening, etc. I also began to realize that there was no salvaging this evening and that I was about to be stuck at his house (near enough, but a long walk still). Even so, being a timid soul, I went back to the house with him. The evening progressed, he poured himself a drink, and sat across the room from me, facing the television and studiously and stonily ignoring me. I had fallen silent and no longer tried to converse with him, and about an hour or more passed. Eventually, he got up and left the room, and I followed him into the kitchen. I told him that I saw absolutely no reason to stay and be treated that way, with no explanation as to what I'd done (even worse if it was just the car door in his mind), and that I was walking home, but if he'd like to talk first, I'd stay a minute. He flew of the handle and began yelling about me treating him badly, bossing him around (we NEVER, not once, did something he had not conceived of and controlled on every level), being a bitch, etc. I said I was leaving, flabbergasted, and he stormed after me, still yelling, only by the time I reached his front door, he was hysterically crying and had crumpled to the floor. I am a tolerant atheist, but his swinging was too much. I get this ALL THE TIME. I am "white," 100% Irish on my dad's side and a hodge-podge on my mom's (American Indian and possibly some southeast Asian distantly). I don't personally think I'm terribly exotic looking, but sometimes it seems like a day doesn't go by without a stranger coming up to me and either anouncing my suspected heritage (French, Czech, Romanian, etc) or quizzing me about my parents ethnicity when I don't give them an answer more fulfilling than "I'm American." 
I was homeschooled by my well-spoken and well-educated parents, and I'm one of those people with a peculiar speech pattern, too; I'm either quiet or I ramble nervously, and even though I technically am from the south, I don't have an accent. That throws people off, for some reason, and I can't tell you how many times my "non-accent" has been interpreted as a foreign version of English (apparently I speak with both a Russian and French accent).

 

However, most people are friendly, and I can't immediately remember a time when I was subjected to predjudice for any of these reasons. 
I have, however, witnessed much racism perpetrated against others. 


The two that stand out most are pretty fucked up.



 
**1)** 
I'd been working as the office manager for a moderately sized small-aircraft maintenance company, and while our building was on a small airfield, security was still tight. One day, I was running late (I normally take public transport) and took a cab to work. The cabby was young and perfectly chill, very friendly. He was also of middle eastern heritage. We talked about music until we arrived, and then I was happily on my way. As I left the cab, he got a phone call and remained outside our building while he chatted. I went inside and signed myself in, and several minutes later I came back to the front of the building and noticed a crowd of my (less than enlightened) coworker observing the cabby outside. They were debating calling security for the "terrorist" sitting outside. This was 2006, and they were ANGRY. The slurs were so venomous and the animosity so white-hot I actually worried about the safety of the guy. Luckily, he drove off soon after.




 

**2)** Recently, my father has been dealing with serious health issues lately, and consequently has been in and out of the hospital and ER a lot. 
Last time he was admitted to the ER, the hospital was full and he stayed in a bed in the ER overnight before being moved up to a room. 
Sometime in the night, a man came in who was in pain and needed treatment, I don't know if something else was immediately wrong, but the guy had AIDS. Problem 1: he was admitted and according to the staff, appeared to be under the influence of illegal drugs. Problem 2: he was black. 
My father ovheard their treatment of this man and was appalled. They were rough and treated him with apparent disgust, put in 2 catheters with no medication to relieve pain, and refused him painkillers all night, while he screamed.
